sections.COMMENTS:
The northwestern termination of the Hellenic Arc subduction system in the Ionian Islands area is characterized by a 100 km wide, NE-SW striking, dextral shear zone which accommodates the different styles and velocities of deformation occurring to the north and south. The main structure in this zone is the Kephallonia-Lefkada strike-slip fault that marks the boundary between the oceanic subduction domain to the south and continental collision to the north, this last caused by the presence of the thick continental Apulian block (Shaw and Jackson, 2010). Another NE-SW strike-slip-fault, crossing the Achaia province, seems to mark the southeastern boundary of the shear zone. NW-SE thrust structures also cohexist in the same area, belonging to the accretionary wedge domain of the Hellenic subduction (Kokinou et al., 2005).
The convergence between Africa and the Aegean plates across the Hellenic Arc is thought to take place at ca. 35 mm/y(Reilinger et al., 2006). GPS velocities of the Aegean plate progressively decrease toward the northwest, where the subduction zone approaches its lateral termination, reaching values of 20-25 mm/y (Hollenstein et al., 2008). North to the Kephallonia-Lefkada fault, convergence between Apulia and the Hellenide domain is in the order of 5-10 mm/y (Hollenstein et al., 2008). The Ionian Island area thus accommodates about 30 mm/y of velocity difference.
Earthquakes show both strike-slip and reverse focal mechanisms (Papazachos et al., 1998; Louvari et al., 1999; Kokinou et al., 2006). P-axis azimuth is around 220Â°N, rotating to 260Â°N while approaching Kephallonia Island (Papazachos et al., 1999).
The largest recorded seismic event associated with this source is the 1983 Mw 7.0 transpressive earthquake, which occurred on the south-western portion of the Kephallonia-Lefkada fault (Louvari et al., 1999). Another event occurred in 2003 with Mw 6.2 and strike-slip kinematics. This event seems to consist of a double rupture on both portions of the Kephallonia-Lefkada structure (Benetatos et al., 2007). The largest recorded seismic event in the whole area is the Mw 7.2 Kephallonia earthquake of 1953, which caused ca. 0.5 m of vertical displacement (Pirazzoli et al., 1994; Stiros et al., 1994). The focal mechanism reported by McKenzie (1972) for the 1953 event is a thrust and the model by Stiros et al. (1994) based on vertical displacement supports this hypothesis. However, Papazachos et al. (1994) associate this earthquake to the southern portion of the Kephallonia-Lefkada strike-slip fault, on the basis of uplift data and the distribution of seismicity. Another large event took place in 1867, with an estimated magnitude of 7.2.
We propose that this Source is located on the southern portion of the Kephallonia-Lefkada structure. The seismic line ION-7 seems to intercept its southern termination about 90 km to the SW off Kephallonia and Zakinthos islands (Kokinou et al., 2005).
We use the distribution of earthquakes (Papazachos et al., 2000, Kokinou et al., 2006) to constrain the depth of this source. The average strike of the source is determined taking into consideration the orientation of geologic and bathymetry features along with focal mechanisms data. Dip and rake were based on data from various authors who analyzed the fault plane solutions and the location of the main earthquakes (Papazachos et al., 1998; Louvari et al., 1999; Kokinou et al., 2006).
We also verified that the source kinematics is consistent with the GPS velocity field.
Slip rate values are obtained by partitioning the geodetic rates among the fault sources, considering that up to 20 mm/y seem to be taken up by this Source according to GPS data (Kahle et al, 1996; Hollenstein et al., 2008).
